title: Portrait of Galileo

original_holder: Oliver Lodge, Pioneers of Science (London and New York: Macmillan, 1893)
caption: Galileo in old age, white-bearded, holding a telescope. The likeness appears to follow the portrait Justus Sustermans painted around 1636, three years after the trial, when Galileo was under house arrest at Arcetri; Lodge's book does not name its source.

caption: Gebler's plan of the suite in the palace of the Holy Office, beside St Peter's and the Vatican gardens, where Galileo was lodged during his interrogations in April 1633: sitting room, bedroom, study and a room for his servant. It is a nineteenth-century reconstruction, not a 1633 drawing.

title: The Moon, from Galileo's 'Sidereus Nuncius'
creator: After Galileo Galilei
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: Galileo, The Sidereal Messenger, trans. Edward Stafford Carlos (London: Rivingtons, 1880)
caption: One of Galileo's telescopic views of the Moon from Sidereus Nuncius (Venice, 1610), showing craters and a rugged edge between light and shadow. It is a copy redrawn for an 1880 English translation, not the 1610 plate itself. Discoveries like this drew Galileo into the Copernican quarrel that ended at his trial in 1633.

title: The Execution of Charles I
creator: Unknown engraver (contemporary broadside print)
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: W. J. Loftie, Whitehall: Historical and Architectural Notes (London: Seeley; New York: Macmillan, 1895)
caption: A print of 1649 showing the beheading of Charles I on the scaffold outside the Banqueting House at Whitehall on 30 January 1649, with the executioner holding up the head to the crowd and soldiers around the scaffold, framed by small portraits. It is a contemporary print but not an eyewitness drawing; such prints were made quickly for sale, many of them on the Continent.

title: Frontispiece of Eikon Basilike
creator: William Marshall (engraver)
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: Eikon Basilike: The Pourtracture of His Sacred Majestie in His Solitudes and Sufferings (London, 1649), as transcribed by Project Gutenberg
caption: William Marshall's frontispiece for Eikon Basilike, the book presented as the king's own meditations and published within days of his execution in 1649. Charles kneels holding a crown of thorns, his earthly crown at his feet and a heavenly crown above. It is royalist propaganda, made to turn the executed king into a martyr.

title: Banqueting Hall, Holbein's Gate, and Treasury

why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).

caption: Whitehall as it looked about 1640, with Inigo Jones's Banqueting House at left and the Tudor Holbein Gate across the street. Charles I walked out of a first-floor window of the Banqueting House onto the scaffold nine years later. Loftie dates the engraving 1640.

title: Death warrant of Bridget Bishop
creator: Court of Oyer and Terminer; signed by William Stoughton (photographic facsimile)
why_public_domain: The plate was first published in 1867 and shows a 1692 manuscript; public domain in the US. The Gutenberg images come from a 1959/1969 photographic reprint, which adds no new copyright to an exact reproduction.
original_holder: Charles W. Upham, Salem Witchcraft, vol. II (Boston: Wiggin and Lunt, 1867); Project Gutenberg text made from the 1959 Frederick Ungar reprint (fourth printing 1969)
caption: The warrant, signed by Chief Justice William Stoughton, ordering Sheriff George Corwin to hang Bridget Bishop, the first person executed after the Salem trials, on 10 June 1692. Upham printed a photograph of the original manuscript, with its wax seal.

title: Sheriff Corwin's return on the warrant
creator: George Corwin, sheriff of Essex County (photographic facsimile)
why_public_domain: The plate was first published in 1867 and shows a 1692 manuscript; public domain in the US. The Gutenberg images come from a 1959/1969 photographic reprint, which adds no new copyright to an exact reproduction.
original_holder: Charles W. Upham, Salem Witchcraft, vol. II (Boston: Wiggin and Lunt, 1867); Project Gutenberg text made from the 1959 Frederick Ungar reprint (fourth printing 1969)
caption: The sheriff's note on the back of the warrant: on 10 June 1692 he took Bridget Bishop from the jail in Salem to the place of execution and hanged her until she was dead. He also wrote that she was buried, then struck those words out. Upham notes that this crossed-out phrase is the only direct evidence of what was done with the bodies.

title: Typical of the Witchcraft Trials
creator: T. H. Matteson (spelled "Mattison" in the book), painting
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: M. V. B. Perley, A Short History of the Salem Village Witchcraft Trials (Salem, Mass.: M. V. B. Perley, 1911)
caption: A mid-nineteenth-century painting of a witchcraft examination: a girl collapses in the courtroom, others throw up their arms, and the accused and the judges are crowded around a table. Perley calls it the only painting of the trials he knew. It was made about 160 years after 1692 and is an imagining, not a record.

title: Increase Mather (father) and Cotton Mather
creator: After portraits painted in their lifetimes (painters not named in the book)

caption: Increase Mather (left) and his son Cotton Mather (right), Boston ministers who both wrote about the 1692 trials: Cotton defending the court in The Wonders of the Invisible World, Increase warning against spectral evidence in Cases of Conscience. Both portraits were painted at other times, not during the trials.

title: Blood on Thunder fording the Red Sea (detail)
creator: After James Gillray (copied by F. W. Fairholt)
date: Gillray's print published 1 March 1788; this copy 1865/1875
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).

caption: Wright's copy of the central part of Gillray's caricature of 1 March 1788, two weeks after the impeachment trial opened: Lord Chancellor Thurlow wades through a sea of blood and corpses carrying Warren Hastings, who clutches his money bags, on his shoulders. It is a satire and takes the prosecution's side.

caption: Edmund Burke, who led the impeachment of Warren Hastings and spoke for four days when the trial opened in Westminster Hall in February 1788. An engraved frontispiece to an 1887 edition of his works; the date of the original painting is not given.

caption: Frances (Fanny) Burney, painted by her cousin Edward Burney a few years before the trial. As Second Keeper of the Robes to Queen Charlotte she attended the opening of the trial in 1788 and recorded Burke's speech and her own sympathy for Hastings in her diary.

caption: Title page of Hone's best-selling 1820 squib for Queen Caroline, here in its 21st edition: the queen sits safe at the top of a ladder while the king tumbles off the bottom. Hone sold it with a cut-out toy ladder, one shilling for both.

title: 'A hundred thousand welcomes!'

why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).
original_holder: [William Hone], The Queen's Matrimonial Ladder, cuts by George Cruikshank, 21st edition (London: William Hone, 1820)
caption: A cut from the same pamphlet, on the queen's return to England in June 1820: a woman in a plumed hat is rowed through rough sea toward white cliffs and a castle flying the flag, while a spouting whale with a bewigged human face, seemingly the king, blocks the way. Caricature, made for her supporters.

title: "Non mi ricordo!": title page
creator: George Cruikshank (woodcut); William Hone (text and publisher)
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).

caption: Hone's 1820 parody of the cross-examination of the Italian witness Teodoro Majocchi, whose repeated 'Non mi ricordo' ('I don't remember') became a London catchphrase. In the cut the king, in the witness box, answers 'Who are you?' This copy is the 31st edition, still from 1820.

title: The courtroom at Charles Town
creator: Unknown newspaper artist (1859 illustrated-newspaper engraving)
why_public_domain: An 1859 newspaper engraving, public domain by age; reproduced in a 1973 US government (National Park Service) booklet, itself not subject to US copyright.
original_holder: National Park Service, John Brown's Raid (National Park Service History Series; Washington: US Government Printing Office, 1973)
caption: An 1859 newspaper engraving of John Brown's trial in the Jefferson County courthouse, with Brown lying on a cot in front of the bench amid a packed crowd. The Park Service notes that the room was smaller than drawn. The booklet does not name the paper; this copy is cropped to remove the booklet's caption and two blank spaces where inset portraits had been.

title: The hanging of John Brown
creator: Unknown newspaper artist (1859 engraving)

original_holder: National Park Service, John Brown's Raid (National Park Service History Series; Washington: US Government Printing Office, 1973)
caption: Troops drawn up in a field outside Charles Town around the scaffold where John Brown was hanged at 11:30 a.m. on 2 December 1859, mounted soldiers in front. Spectators were kept away, so newspaper artists worked largely from reports.

title: John Brown's last note
creator: John Brown
why_public_domain: Written in 1859; public domain by age. Reproduced in a 1973 US government (National Park Service) booklet, not subject to US copyright.
original_holder: National Park Service, John Brown's Raid (National Park Service History Series; Washington: US Government Printing Office, 1973)
caption: The note Brown handed to a guard on the morning of his execution: 'I John Brown am now quite certain that the crimes of this guilty, land: will never be purged away; but with Blood.' The booklet prints it as handwriting but does not say whether this is a photograph of the original or a redrawn copy.

caption: Henry A. Wise, governor of Virginia in 1859, who questioned Brown after his capture, insisted on a Virginia trial and refused to commute the sentence. The photograph's date is not given; it appears in a biography of John Quincy Adams because Wise had been Adams's opponent in Congress.

creator: After Alfred Dreyfus
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).

title: M. Bertillon's plan of expert proof
creator: After Alphonse Bertillon
why_public_domain: Published before 1929; long out of copyright (public domain in the US, and the creators died more than 70 years ago).

It was printed in the English report of Zola's libel trial in 1898, where Bertillon told the court it was only a scheme for one point of his evidence. His method was later discredited.

title: Courtroom 600 on the opening day of the Doctors' Trial
creator: US Army photographer (not named)
why_public_domain: A work of the United States government (photograph by US military photographers, printed by the US Government Printing Office); not subject to copyright in the US.
original_holder: Trials of War Criminals before the Nuernberg Military Tribunals under Control Council Law No. 10, vol. I (Washington: US Government Printing Office, 1949)
caption: The courtroom in the Nuremberg Palace of Justice, seen from above with judges, defendants and lawyers in their places and Telford Taylor at the lectern. It is not the trial of Göring and the others: it shows the first of the later American trials, which opened two months after the International Military Tribunal gave its judgment, in the same room.

title: The Japanese surrender, Tokyo Bay
creator: US military photographer (not named)
why_public_domain: A photograph taken by US military personnel on duty (credited to the US National Archives); a US government work, not subject to US copyright. Taken from OpenStax World History vol. 2, whose own text is under a Creative Commons licence; the photograph itself is public domain.
original_holder: OpenStax, World History, Volume 2: from 1400 (Houston: OpenStax, Rice University, 2022), figure "The Japanese Surrender"; credited to the US National Archives
caption: General Umezu Yoshijirō signs the instrument of surrender for the Japanese armed forces on the USS Missouri on 2 September 1945, with Allied officers lined up behind General MacArthur at the microphones. Umezu, and Shigemitsu Mamoru, who signed for the government that morning, were later both defendants at the Tokyo trial.
